moment: A song got stuck in my head all day and I couldn’t make it stop.
question: Why do songs get stuck in my head?
summary: Imagining music uses many of the same areas as hearing it. A short, catchy fragment can loop on its own, especially when your mind is idle.

beats.title: The trigger
beats.text: Maybe you heard the song this morning, or a word reminded you of it. Earworms are often set off by recent listening, a memory, or even a mood.

beats.title: Hearing without sound
beats.text: Your auditory cortex starts recreating the tune. Imagining music activates many of the same areas as actually hearing it, which is why an earworm can feel so real.

beats.title: The hook loops
beats.text: It’s usually just a short fragment, often the chorus. Areas that plan speech and movement can join in, as if you’re silently singing along, and that helps keep the loop going.

beats.title: An idle mind
beats.text: Earworms tend to show up when your attention isn’t busy, like when you’re walking or washing up. With nothing else to grab your focus, the loop takes centre stage.

beats.title: Trying not to think of it
beats.text: Telling yourself to stop can backfire. To check whether the song has gone, your brain has to look for it, which can bring it right back.

whyItFelt: Catchy songs tend to have simple, repetitive melodies with a slightly unusual twist, which makes them easy to replay. One idea is that the fragment feels unfinished, so your brain keeps returning to it, a bit like a question waiting for an answer.

tryThis.title: Listen to the whole song
tryThis.text: Hearing it all the way through may help close the loop.

tryThis.title: Chew gum
tryThis.text: In one study, chewing gum reduced earworms, possibly because it keeps busy the mouth and jaw muscles used for silent singing.

tryThis.title: Give your brain a puzzle
tryThis.text: A moderately hard task, like anagrams or sudoku, can crowd the song out. Too easy and it won’t work; too hard and the song creeps back.

finePrint: Surveys suggest most people get an earworm at least once a week, so this is completely normal.
Brain imaging shows imagined and heard music overlap, but the exact circuitry of earworms is still being studied.
